A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ZOO-Prune and contain readable text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices. Their shared method and experiments can be matched reliably despite substantial presentation changes.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark evaluations, sensitivity correlations, ablations, efficiency measurements, and qualitative results in Sections 3–4 and the appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains those original empirical results and adds attention-scoring comparisons, encoder-layer sensitivity experiments, and qualitative analyses.

M1.justification: Section 3 and Algorithm 1 retain the same normalized perturbations, symmetric finite differences, sensitivity normalization, and multiplicative sensitivity–diversity selection. Projector-based estimation and the LLaVA-NeXT rank-128 factorization already appear in v1. The new encoder-layer experiments evaluate alternatives without changing the proposed procedure.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same nine image-language benchmarks and retain the same task coverage. MMMU and SEED disappear from v2's main Table 1 but remain in Appendix Table B. The new analyses use existing benchmarks; video, 3D, and interactive-agent applications remain future work.

E2.justification: v2 Table 1 adds ToMe, HiRED, and PyramidDrop to the LLaVA-1.5-7B comparison at all three token budgets, retaining the earlier comparators. New controlled comparisons evaluate T2V and V2V attention variants with and without diversity. Appendix Figure D also adds VisionZip to qualitative cases previously comparing only DivPrune and ZOO-Prune.

E3.justification: Existing model configurations, pruning budgets, zero-shot evaluation, and default hyperparameters remain unchanged. New analyses introduce layer-wise sensitivity controls and specified T2V/V2V scoring procedures. Main Table 1 averages seven benchmarks, while the original nine-benchmark summary remains in Appendix B. Efficiency evaluation is now described as using POPE rather than ScienceQA; this establishes a reported setting revision, not that measurements were rerun.

E4.justification: The original fusion and hyperparameter ablations remain. v2 adds attention-versus-sensitivity comparisons in Figures 5–6, a systematic comparison of 13 encoder layers against the projector in Table D and Figure B, and expanded GQA case studies. Failure examples retain boy/baby but replace lady/woman with a mug/glass confusion in clutter.

E5.justification: The 50-sample correlation analysis and KDE reporting remain unchanged. Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests for benchmark performance. Perturbation-direction counts describe the estimator, not repeated experimental runs.

E6.justification: Original Tables 1–5 retain their scores in v2 Tables B, C, 3, 2, and 4. Substantial new results cover added baselines, attention variants, and encoder layers; Table D reports 95.4% average retention for the projector versus 89.1% for Layer 1 at 160 tokens. Main Table 1's 95.20% versus v1's 95.5% reflects different benchmark aggregation, not deterioration. The 13B DivPrune gap is corrected from 1.7 to 1.1 percentage points, but new Appendix D.1 prose mislabels GQA's 59.49 as SQA, whose table value is 68.91.

T1.justification: The sensitivity definition, Proposition 3.1/B.1, assumptions, and Appendix B Taylor-expansion argument remain substantively identical, including the stated O(h²) approximation. Equations are split and renumbered without new mathematical reasoning.

C1.justification: The central training-free sensitivity–diversity contribution and headline 94.4% pruning and 2.30× speedup claims remain. v2's conclusion additionally claims that sensitivity rankings preserve the same task-critical regions across models under extreme pruning, introducing a more specific cross-model consistency claim.

C2.justification: v1 treats the illustrated failures as semantically correct answers unfairly penalized by exact matching. v2 instead acknowledges lost fine-grained cues and confusion in clutter as recognition limitations. It adds interpretations of attention positional bias and the encoder-layer results, expands architectural and modality boundaries in Appendix F, and removes the earlier perturbation-overhead caveat and proposal to use roughly four perturbations.

D1.justification: v2 removes v1's model-checkpoint links, including the explicit Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct-AWQ identification, the lmms-eval repository link, and the promised source-code release statement. Hardware, batch size, pruning implementation, and default hyperparameters remain documented. These are disclosure changes, not evidence of a changed checkpoint or actual code availability.

R1.justification: v2 adds references including HiRED, ToMe, PyramidDrop, Balanced Token Pruning, GreedyPrune, Honeybee, Pargo, and attention-interpretability work. These extend support for the existing argument about attention reliability and projector alignment without substantially redefining the paper's research positioning.

P1.justification: The experimental and appendix narrative is substantially reorganized: the 13B discussion moves into expanded Appendix D, qualitative discussion is relocated and rewritten, failure analysis and the conclusion are revised, and limitations become Appendix F. The former reproducibility statement and LLM writing-assistance section are removed. The title also gains the ZOO-Prune prefix.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column layout and substantially restructures the displays. It retains the original full benchmark tables in the appendices, expands the main comparator table, adds attention and encoder-layer figures, and replaces efficiency bars with performance–latency scatter and bubble plots. Qualitative panels are expanded and redesigned with light masks and highlighted regions.

improvement.justification: The new attention controls and encoder-layer comparison provide useful additional support for the retained design choices, while the revised failure analysis is more candid than v1's dismissal of errors. These improve an already extensive evaluation. The net gain is limited by removed checkpoint/access information and new prose–table inconsistencies, notably the SQA/GQA mix-up in Appendix D.1.
